        <h3 dir="auto">Discussion Type</h3>
<p dir="auto">Product Feedback</p>
<h3 dir="auto">Discussion Content</h3>
<p dir="auto">Hello everyone,</p>
<p dir="auto">I'm currently working on a Slither.io private server written in C++, hosted on a VPS. The server is based on Protocol 14 and was originally developed by a friend of mine, but unfortunately he abandoned the project before it reached a stable state.</p>
<p dir="auto">The server is functional and players can connect, move, eat food, grow, and interact with each other. However, there are still several issues that prevent it from behaving like the official Slither.io servers.</p>
<p dir="auto">Current Problems</p>
<p dir="auto">Some of the issues we've identified so far include:</p>
<p dir="auto">Snake rotation does not feel smooth or accurate.<br>
Turning speed differs from official servers.<br>
Movement speed feels inconsistent compared to official gameplay.<br>
Snakes sometimes appear to "shake" or "vibrate" while moving.<br>
Position updates can look jittery under certain conditions.<br>
Tick rate / update timing may not match the original game.<br>
Body segments do not always follow the head smoothly.<br>
Boosting behavior does not perfectly match official servers.<br>
Collision detection may occasionally feel inaccurate.<br>
Spawn behavior still needs improvement.<br>
Network synchronization between client and server needs refinement.<br>
Some protocol packets may not be implemented exactly as the original game.<br>
Interpolation and prediction behavior are likely different from the official implementation.<br>
What I'm Looking For</p>
<p dir="auto">I'm trying to make the server behave as closely as possible to the official Slither.io experience.</p>
<p dir="auto">If you have experience with:</p>
<p dir="auto">Slither.io protocol reverse engineering<br>
Game networking<br>
Real-time multiplayer servers<br>
C++<br>
Entity interpolation and movement systems<br>
Tick-based game loops</p>
<p dir="auto">your help would be greatly appreciated.</p>
<p dir="auto">Testing</p>
<p dir="auto">You can compare behavior by:</p>
<p dir="auto">Connecting to an official Slither.io server.<br>
Using NTL Mod or another client modification for comparison.<br>
Connecting to my private server running on VPS/Linux.<br>
Comparing movement, rotation, speed, boosting, collisions, and overall gameplay feel.<br>
Repository & Resources</p>
<p dir="auto">I will provide:</p>
<p dir="auto">The server repository.<br>
Protocol 14 documentation.<br>
A JavaScript implementation of the Protocol 14 client.<br>
Access information for testing.</p>
<p dir="auto">Unfortunately, some people who already have working private Slither.io servers have chosen not to share information or help newer developers. Because of that, I'm hoping to collaborate with the community and learn from others who are interested in the project.</p>
<p dir="auto">Any contribution, suggestion, code review, testing, or technical advice would be greatly appreciated.</p>
<p dir="auto">Thank you very much for your time and support! 🙂<br>
<a href="https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28858259/protocol14.js">protocol14.js</a></p>
<p dir="auto">Here is the server that my friend created: <a href="https://github.com/bots2020/servidor_slither">https://github.com/bots2020/servidor_slither</a></p>

        <hr>
<p dir="auto">Happy to help — these are classic real-time multiplayer server problems. Let me address each category systematically.</p>
<hr>
<h2 dir="auto">1. Movement & Rotation Smoothness</h2>
<p dir="auto">The shake/vibrate and jitter issues almost always come from one of two things: <strong>inconsistent tick rate</strong> or <strong>floating point accumulation error</strong>.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Fix tick rate first — use a fixed timestep loop:</strong></p>
<div class="highlight highlight-source-c++ notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="#include <chrono>

const double TICK_RATE = 1.0 / 25.0; // Slither uses ~25 ticks/sec

void GameLoop() {
    using clock = std::chrono::steady_clock;
    auto lastTime = clock::now();
    double accumulator = 0.0;

    while (running) {
        auto now = clock::now();
        double deltaTime = std::chrono::duration<double>(now - lastTime).count();
        lastTime = now;

        accumulator += deltaTime;

        while (accumulator >= TICK_RATE) {
            update(TICK_RATE); // fixed step update
            accumulator -= TICK_RATE;
        }

        // render/broadcast interpolated state
        broadcast(accumulator / TICK_RATE); // alpha for interpolation
    }
}"><pre class="notranslate">#<span class="pl-k">include</span> <span class="pl-s"><span class="pl-pds"><</span>chrono<span class="pl-pds">></span></span>

<span class="pl-k">const</span> <span class="pl-k">double</span> <span class="pl-c1">TICK_RATE</span> = <span class="pl-c1">1.0</span> / <span class="pl-c1">25.0</span>; <span class="pl-c"><span class="pl-c">//</span> Slither uses ~25 ticks/sec</span>

<span class="pl-k">void</span> <span class="pl-en">GameLoop</span>() {
    <span class="pl-k">using</span> clock = std::chrono::steady_clock;
    <span class="pl-k">auto</span> lastTime = <span class="pl-c1">clock::now</span>();
    <span class="pl-k">double</span> accumulator = <span class="pl-c1">0.0</span>;

    <span class="pl-k">while</span> (running) {
        <span class="pl-k">auto</span> now = <span class="pl-c1">clock::now</span>();
        <span class="pl-k">double</span> deltaTime = std::chrono::duration<<span class="pl-k">double</span>>(now - lastTime).<span class="pl-c1">count</span>();
        lastTime = now;

        accumulator += deltaTime;

        <span class="pl-k">while</span> (accumulator >= <span class="pl-c1">TICK_RATE</span>) {
            <span class="pl-c1">update</span>(<span class="pl-c1">TICK_RATE</span>); <span class="pl-c"><span class="pl-c">//</span> fixed step update</span>
            accumulator -= <span class="pl-c1">TICK_RATE</span>;
        }

        <span class="pl-c"><span class="pl-c">//</span> render/broadcast interpolated state</span>
        <span class="pl-c1">broadcast</span>(accumulator / <span class="pl-c1">TICK_RATE</span>); <span class="pl-c"><span class="pl-c">//</span> alpha for interpolation</span>
    }
}</pre></div>
<p dir="auto">Never pass raw <code class="notranslate">deltaTime</code> into your physics — always use a fixed step. Variable delta is what causes the shake.</p>
<hr>
<h2 dir="auto">2. Snake Rotation — Angular Velocity Cap</h2>
<p dir="auto">Slither doesn't allow instant direction changes. It caps angular velocity. The official protocol uses approximately <strong>0.2 radians per tick</strong> as the max turn rate.</p>
<div class="highlight highlight-source-c++ notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="const float MAX_TURN_RATE = 0.2f; // radians per tick

void updateSnakeDirection(Snake& snake, float targetAngle) {
    float diff = targetAngle - snake.angle;
    
    // Normalize to [-PI, PI]
    while (diff > M_PI)  diff -= 2.0f * M_PI;
    while (diff < -M_PI) diff += 2.0f * M_PI;
    
    // Clamp to max turn rate
    diff = std::clamp(diff, -MAX_TURN_RATE, MAX_TURN_RATE);
    
    snake.angle += diff;
}"><pre class="notranslate"><span class="pl-k">const</span> <span class="pl-k">float</span> <span class="pl-c1">MAX_TURN_RATE</span> = <span class="pl-c1">0</span>.<span class="pl-c1">2f</span>; <span class="pl-c"><span class="pl-c">//</span> radians per tick</span>

<span class="pl-k">void</span> <span class="pl-en">updateSnakeDirection</span>(Snake& snake, <span class="pl-k">float</span> targetAngle) {
    <span class="pl-k">float</span> diff = targetAngle - snake.<span class="pl-smi">angle</span>;
    
    <span class="pl-c"><span class="pl-c">//</span> Normalize to [-PI, PI]</span>
    <span class="pl-k">while</span> (diff > <span class="pl-c1">M_PI</span>)  diff -= <span class="pl-c1">2</span>.<span class="pl-c1">0f</span> * <span class="pl-c1">M_PI</span>;

<hr>
<h2 dir="auto">3. Body Segment Following</h2>
<p dir="auto">Segments should follow the <strong>path the head traced</strong>, not follow the segment in front of them directly. Direct following causes accordion/bunching artifacts.</p>
<p dir="auto">Use a <strong>path buffer</strong> approach:</p>
<div class="highlight highlight-source-c++ notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="struct PathPoint {

    float totalDist = 0.0f;
    
    for (int i = 0; i < snake.segments.size(); i++) {
        float targetDist = (i + 1) * snake.segmentSpacing;
        
        // Walk back through path history to find correct position
        for (int j = 0; j < snake.pathHistory.size() - 1; j++) {
            auto& p1 = snake.pathHistory[j];
            auto& p2 = snake.pathHistory[j + 1];

<hr>
<h2 dir="auto">4. Boost Behavior</h2>
<p dir="auto">During boost, Slither does two things simultaneously:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li><strong>Increases speed</strong> (roughly 2× base speed)</li>
<li><strong>Decreases snake length</strong> (burns mass)</li>

<hr>
<h2 dir="auto">5. Client-Side Interpolation (reduce jitter on clients)</h2>
<p dir="auto">Even with a perfect server, clients will see jitter if you're sending raw positions. Send positions every tick but have clients <strong>interpolate between the last two received states</strong>:</p>
<div class="highlight highlight-source-c++ notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="// Server: send state snapshot every tick

<p dir="auto">100ms interpolation buffer is standard for games of this type. It trades a tiny bit of latency for smooth visuals.</p>
<hr>
<h2 dir="auto">6. Protocol 14 Packet Timing</h2>
<p dir="auto">From looking at your repo briefly — make sure position update packets are sent <strong>every tick</strong> for nearby snakes and <strong>throttled</strong> for distant ones. Slither uses a sector/zone system where snakes far from the viewport get lower update frequency. Sending full-world updates every tick to every client is the most common cause of network sync issues on private servers.</p>
<hr>
<h2 dir="auto">Suggested debugging order</h2>
<ol dir="auto">
<li>Fix the game loop to fixed timestep first — this alone will fix 50% of your issues</li>
<li>Tune <code class="notranslate">MAX_TURN_RATE</code> to match official feel</li>
<li>Implement path-based segment following</li>
<li>Fix boost mass drain + food ejection</li>
<li>Add client interpolation buffer</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Happy to look at specific sections of your code if you share the relevant movement/tick files from the repo. What does your current game loop look like?</p>

        <p dir="auto">Perfect, thank you very much for taking the time to help me. I really appreciate it.</p>
<p dir="auto">The main server-related files in the project are:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li><code class="notranslate">src/game/world.cc</code></li>
<li><code class="notranslate">src/server/server.h</code></li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Repository:<br>
<a href="https://github.com/bots2020/servidor_slither/tree/main/servidor_slither-main">https://github.com/bots2020/servidor_slither/tree/main/servidor_slither-main</a></p>
<p dir="auto">Here are the answers to your questions:</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>1)</strong> Yes. I'm hosting the server on an Azure VPS. The goal is to create a private server where friends can play together and also organize matches against players from other teams.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>2)</strong> This same project already exists in other countries, and those servers are fully functional. As far as I know, they usually handle around 20 to 30 concurrent players without any issues.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>3)</strong> A friend of mine has already fixed several important issues, especially those related to snake rotation and movement. However, there are still many bugs that we're trying to solve so the gameplay matches the original Slither.io server as closely as possible.</p>
<p dir="auto">Some of the remaining issues are:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>When a player spawns, the snake's body appears glitched or cut near the tail.</li>
<li>Snake-to-snake collision is not accurate; sometimes snakes pass through each other.</li>
<li>When the snake reaches around <strong>50k mass</strong>, turning becomes much slower and heavier than it should. On the official servers the behavior is noticeably different, so we believe our movement logic is still not identical.</li>
<li>Boost behavior also feels wrong. It activates much faster than it does on the official servers.</li>
<li>Right now, our server only works with a specific client (mod) that supports our protocol. We'd really like the server to be compatible with any client, such as <strong>NTL Slither</strong>, <strong>Frontier Slither</strong>, <strong>Vlither</strong>, and other mods, without crashing or refusing the connection.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Our goal is to replicate the original server behavior as accurately as possible. The only intentional difference is that we reduced the map size and added a Battle Royale-style dome for matches between friends and rival teams.</p>
<p dir="auto">One detail that might be important: a friend of mine already used <strong>Wireshark</strong> to analyze the traffic from one of the private US servers. Thanks to that, we were able to replicate a large part of the server's behavior and fix several issues.</p>
<p dir="auto">The problem is that we've reached a point where packet analysis alone isn't enough. The most important mechanics seem to be implemented entirely in the server itself, such as the exact collision logic, body synchronization, smooth turning, boost behavior, and other internal algorithms that simply can't be reconstructed by looking at network traffic alone. That's where we're currently stuck.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>4)</strong> I have a friend who is a programmer, and he has already fixed many bugs in both the mods and the server. However, these more complex mechanics are still very difficult to reproduce. We know that some private US servers have managed to make their gameplay almost identical to the official Slither.io servers, but unfortunately they don't like sharing how they achieved it.</p>
<p dir="auto">If you have any suggestions about where we should start investigating these mechanics, or if you know of any techniques that could help us reproduce the original server behavior more accurately, I would really appreciate your advice. Any guidance would be a huge help.</p>
